name: Broker overflow loads to third-party carriers
summary: When the carrier's own trucks cannot take a customer's load, a brokerage agent finds another trucking company to haul it, earning the gap between the customer rate and the rate paid to that carrier. The agent calls carriers it already uses or posts the load on a load board, vets new carriers, sends a rate confirmation, tracks the load to delivery and collects the proof of delivery, and accounts payable matches the carrier's invoice before payment. Margins are thin, rates move fast in tight markets, and no-shows, delays and carriers using stolen identities to double broker loads add rework and risk.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with a small brokerage desk inside its truckload division that covers overflow loads in Canada and to and from the US.
baseline.notes: One case is one brokered load from release by the load planner to the carrier invoice approved for payment; the payment run itself is in accounts payable.

trigger: A booked customer load cannot be covered by a company driver or owner-operator and the load planner releases it to brokerage.
end_state: The load is delivered, the trip record is with billing and the carrier invoice is approved for payment, or payment is held after suspected fraud.

volume.seasonality: Highest in the September to mid-December peak and in spring 2021 to early 2022 when capacity was tight; low in spring 2020.

evidence.note: Follows the organisation file. At about CAD 2,500 per load (TIA average truckload invoice of USD 1,997 in Q4 2020 converted at about 1.27) 600 loads a month is about CAD 18 million a year, about 3% of revenue, against the organisation file's statement that brokerage is about 6% of revenue.

surge.cause: Autumn shipping peak (September to mid-December retail and industrial restocking)

evidence.note: Copied from the organisation file's process map; author's estimate of size.
About 115 minutes of agent time per load on 600 loads a month is about 8.5 FTE; the organisation file has 12 agents, who also quote and keep carrier relationships.
Release decisions; author's estimate.
Above-target rate approvals on about 7% of loads; author's estimate.
Vendor set-up and invoice matching; author's estimate.
Cross-border checks on about 35% of loads; author's estimate.
Delay and accessorial calls on about 12% of loads; author's estimate.
Suspected fraud on about 1% of loads; author's estimate.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Email, phone system and contact centre software
ERP general ledger, payables and receivables
eManifest service provider (CBSA ACI and US CBP ACE)
Document imaging for bills of lading and delivery receipts

steps.name: Release an uncovered load to brokerage
steps.description: The truckload load planner looks at a booked load that no company driver or owner-operator can reach before the pickup appointment, for example in a lane the fleet rarely runs or during the autumn peak, and flags it in the TMS as released to brokerage.

error.defect_description: A load released too late to cover at a sensible rate.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the load and set a target buy rate
steps.description: The brokerage agent opens the load in the TMS, reads the customer rate, equipment, weight, appointments and border crossing, looks up what was paid on the lane before and the current load-board rate, and sets the most the carrier can be paid while keeping a margin of about 12% to 15%.

evidence.note: TIA truckload brokerage gross margins of 11.4% to 15.2% in 2019-2020 set the target; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Call carriers on the approved list
steps.description: The agent phones or emails carriers already set up and known to run the lane, offering the load at or below the target rate. About half of loads are covered this way.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate. Share covered from the approved list is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Post the load on a load board
steps.description: The agent posts the lane, dates, equipment and a rate or 'call for rate' on a load board used in Canada and the US, and watches for calls.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Take carrier calls and negotiate the rate
steps.description: The agent takes calls from carriers and dispatchers who saw the posting, asks for their MC or safety number, truck location and empty time, and negotiates the rate. During tight markets in 2021 the agent may call back several times as rates rise.

next.condition: carrier wants more than the target rate

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve a buy rate above target
steps.description: The truckload operations manager decides whether to pay above the target, cutting or losing the margin, to protect a customer's service, or to go back to the customer for a higher rate.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority: below-margin brokered loads approved by the operations manager

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Vet the new carrier
steps.description: The agent checks the carrier's operating authority and safety rating (FMCSA records for US authority, the provincial safety rating for Canadian carriers), calls the insurer to confirm liability and cargo cover, checks the authority's age, the address and email domain, and calls back on the carrier's main number.

error.defect_description: A carrier using a stolen identity or planning to double broker passes the checks.

control.basis: Company carrier selection policy: authority, safety rating and insurance verified before tender

evidence.note: Vetting checks from Transport Topics and TIA; pass rate and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set up the new carrier as a vendor
steps.description: The accounts payable clerk enters the carrier's legal name, GST number or US tax form, remit-to address and bank details from the signed broker-carrier agreement into the ERP, and confirms bank details by phone.

error.defect_description: Wrong remit-to or bank details entered.

control.basis: Internal control: carrier bank details entered by accounts payable, not by the agent who books the load

evidence.note: Vendor set-up by accounts payable is a common control; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the rate confirmation
steps.description: The agent builds the rate confirmation in the TMS with the pickup and delivery details, the agreed rate, accessorial rules, tracking and paperwork requirements, and emails it to the carrier.

error.defect_description: Wrong appointment time or rate typed on the confirmation.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Carrier signs and returns the rate confirmation
steps.description: The carrier's dispatcher signs the rate confirmation and returns it with the driver's name, cell number, tractor and trailer numbers.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate. Cross-border share is the author's estimate for a carrier with US lanes.

steps.name: Confirm customs filings for a cross-border load
steps.description: The cross-border customs coordinator checks that the carrier has filed its eManifest with CBSA or US CBP before arrival and that the customs broker has the PARS or PAPS number for the shipment, and sends the carrier the customs paperwork.

control.basis: CBSA Advance Commercial Information (eManifest) and US CBP ACE eManifest requirements for highway carriers

evidence.note: CBSA ACI eManifest and US ACE eManifest must be sent before the truck reaches the border; texts not opened by this author, so tier C.

steps.name: Carrier picks up the load
steps.description: The carrier's truck travels to the shipper and loads at the appointment. A carrier that does not show up leaves the agent to re-cover the load at short notice.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate. No-show share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Track the load with check calls
steps.description: The agent calls or texts the driver at pickup, once a day in transit and before delivery, or follows a tracking link, and updates the load status in the TMS so customer service can answer the shipper.

next.condition: truck or driver does not match the rate confirmation

evidence.note: Tracking and identity checks as anti-fraud practice; times and shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Handle a delay, detention or damage with the customer
steps.description: The truckload customer service representative tells the shipper or consignee about the delay, for example a winter highway closure or a long wait at the dock, rebooks the appointment, and records detention or other accessorial charges to bill and to pay the carrier.

evidence.note: Winter storms and dock waits are common causes of delay; shares and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm delivery and collect the proof of delivery
steps.description: The agent confirms delivery with the driver or consignee and asks the carrier to email the signed bill of lading and proof of delivery, which the agent attaches to the load in the imaging system.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter the trip record and carrier cost for billing
steps.description: The agent completes the load in the TMS with delivery date, accessorials and the carrier cost, which releases it to billing to invoice the customer and records the expected carrier payable.

error.defect_description: Accessorial or carrier cost entered wrong or missed.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Receive the carrier's invoice
steps.description: The carrier mails or emails its invoice with the bill of lading and proof of delivery. Many small carriers choose quick-pay at a discount or factor their invoices, which changes who is paid.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Match the carrier invoice to the rate confirmation and POD
steps.description: The accounts payable clerk matches the invoice amount with the signed rate confirmation, the accessorials approved in the TMS and the proof of delivery, checks the remit-to against the vendor record, and approves the invoice for the next payment run.

control.basis: Internal control over financial reporting: match of carrier invoice, rate confirmation and proof of delivery before payment

next.condition: amount or paperwork does not match

evidence.note: Matching invoices to rate confirmations is common practice; mismatch share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Resolve the invoice discrepancy
steps.description: The agent reviews the disputed amount, usually detention, a lumper fee or an extra stop, calls the carrier, and either approves the extra charge in the TMS or asks the carrier for a corrected invoice.

evidence.note: Truckload brokerage practice at an asset-based Canadian carrier 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Investigate a suspected double broker or identity theft
steps.description: The cargo security coordinator calls the carrier on its registered main number, checks whether the truck at the shipper belongs to the carrier on the rate confirmation, and if not, holds the payment, warns the customer and reports the case.

control.basis: Company cargo security policy: payment held until the hauling carrier is confirmed

evidence.note: Double brokering rose from late 2022; holding payment until the hauling carrier is identified is described by Transport Topics. Share and times are the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Load board needed
exceptions.description: No approved carrier takes the load, so the agent posts it and vets a new carrier.

exceptions.name: Rate above target
exceptions.description: The only available carrier wants more than the target rate and the operations manager approves or refuses.

exceptions.name: Carrier no-show
exceptions.description: The carrier does not arrive and the load is re-posted at short notice.

exceptions.name: Delay or detention
exceptions.description: Weather or dock waits delay the load; customer service rebooks and records accessorials.

exceptions.name: Invoice mismatch
exceptions.description: The carrier invoice does not match the rate confirmation, usually because of accessorials.

exceptions.name: Suspected double brokering
exceptions.description: The truck at pickup is not the contracted carrier's; payment is held and security investigates.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from release to brokerage to carrier invoice approved
benchmarks.population: Brokered truckload loads at an asset-based carrier

evidence.note: Author's estimate: same or next day to cover, one to three days in transit, and several days for the carrier to invoice and accounts payable to match.

benchmarks.population: TIA member brokers, Q4 2019 to Q4 2020

evidence.note: Needed for the carrier to broker loads under US broker authority.

pain_points.description: Covering loads off the load board takes many calls and rate rounds, and vetting each new carrier by phone adds time.

evidence.note: Vetting steps from Transport Topics and TIA; effort is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Carriers using stolen identities and double brokering rose from late 2022, so checks that passed a carrier may still let a fraudster through.
Thin margins mean a single above-target buy or an unbilled detention charge wipes out the profit on a load.

evidence.note: Margins of 11% to 15% from TIA data.

pain_points.description: Carrier invoices arrive days after delivery and often disagree with the rate confirmation on accessorials.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Truckload brokerage margins in Q4 lowest in 2 years: TIA
sources.supports: TIA quarterly data: truckload brokerage gross margin 11.4% in Q4 2020, down from 12.4% in Q3 2020 and 15.2% in Q4 2019; average truckload invoice USD 1,997 per load in Q4 2020.

sources.title: 49 CFR 387.307 - Property broker surety bond or trust fund
sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (US Code of Federal Regulations)
sources.supports: A property broker must hold a USD 75,000 surety bond (Form BMC-84) or trust fund (Form BMC-85).

sources.title: Reports of Double-Brokering Increase
sources.supports: TIA Watchdog reports of double brokering rose from December 2022; Truckstop saw a 400% rise in complaints in Q4 2022 and Q1 2023; brokers vet carriers by operating history, inspection records, insurance confirmation with the insurer, address and email-domain checks, call-backs to the carrier's main number and holding payment until the hauling carrier is identified.

sources.title: Carrier vetting red flags brokers should know
sources.supports: Broker carrier-vetting steps: verify USDOT and MC numbers against name and address, check contact details and email domain, require proof of insurance, check authority age and work history, take time over verification. A later article describing checks that were already common.

assumptions: Volume follows the organisation file (450 to 850 loads a month). That volume implies brokerage revenue of about 3% of company revenue, not the 6% the organisation file states; one of the two is off by about a factor of two.
The process ends when the carrier invoice is approved; payment terms (often 30 days, or quick-pay at a discount) are in accounts payable.
Margins use US TIA figures; Canadian brokerage margins in the period are assumed similar.
The carrier is assumed to hold US broker authority with the USD 75,000 bond for loads it brokers in the US; Canadian provincial broker rules are not modelled.
Customs and eManifest rules are described from general knowledge; the CBSA page cited in the organisation file was not opened by this author.
The simulated median of about 10 days is above the 8-day estimate because carrier invoices arrive up to a week after delivery; the estimate itself is tier C, so the gap is left as it is.
The neighbouring tender workflow sends about 6.5% of truckload tenders to brokerage, about 600 loads a month on 9,500 tenders, which supports the volume used here.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file. Third-party trucks are not company resources, so no resources are listed.
